newsitem.title: USA: FAA makes airline safety data available to public.
newsitem.headline: FAA makes airline safety data available to public.

text.p: U.S. safety regulators said on Wednesday that starting next month they will make public a wide variety of new airline safety information so the public can know if a carrier has a good safety record.

The action by the Federal Aviation Administration follows calls by Congress and consumer advocates, as well as the crash last May of ValuJet Inc. Flight 592 near Miami, killing all 110 people on board.
ValuJet later was disclosed to have been under FAA investigation for a series of FAA airworthiness violations.

Under the new FAA policy, starting on Feb. 1 the agency will make public enforcement actions in the safety and security area that seek civil penalities of $50,000 or more, as well as major regulatory actions such as the revocation of flying certificates.

Acting FAA Administrator Linda Daschle said that while passengers want to know if a plane will arrive on time, and if not, why, "every passenger also wants to know if the carrier had a good safety record and whether it meets federal aviation safety requirments."

Daschle said that on Feb. 28 the FAA will open a dedicated Internet page for safety data, including material such as accident and incident data previously available only through Freedom of Information Act requests.
More information will be put on the Internet page during the year, she said, including certification dates of aircraft and types of aircraft flown.
Sen. Ron Wyden, an Oregon Democrat and one of those behind the FAA action, said that until now people had to wade through red tape to get safety information.

"For the first time, the flying public will be able to conveniently determine if their airline has major safety problems. From now on, aviation safety secrets are going public," Wyden said in a statement.

But the U.S. Air Transport Association expressed concern about putting safety information on the Internet, saying it would be difficult for people to go into the net and make a judgment on the safety of any one airline.
The trade association of major U.S. carriers said the information could imply a safety ranking and lead to competition among the carriers over safety.

It said that airlines now competed in many areas, but not on safety, and airlines shared their safety information with other carriers. "To inject competition into that process is wrong," the ATA said.

Daschle said that in developing the policy, the FAA had to strike a balance between the public's right to know and the important need to protect information shared with the agency on a voluntary basis that helps advance the cause of safety.

She said the FAA believes safety and security information given voluntarily should be protected from disclosure so the FAA can encourage safety through disclosure and not endanger safety by discouraging anyone from telling the agency something it ought to know.

"The FAA intends to make as much information public as possible, while protecting key information it receives voluntarily so that continued reporting that will lead to higher levels of safety can be encouraged," she said.
Daschle also said the FAA would put on its Internet page information that will help consumers better understand how impressive the U.S. safety record is -- the world's best.
FAA officials said they discussed with Wyden the idea of ranking airlines by safety, but dropped that idea on grounds past safety information was not a key to future safety.
They said accidents of aircraft flying under FAA rules were just that -- "accidents" -- and there was no way the past could predict the future.
